### 2026-10-12 — Q-868 built the simple way (#3689); a 9-round regex reader abandoned

**What the admin asked:** "Create an racing game for Nokia c 2-01" asked for the classic game that came on that phone. It did not ask for a game meant to run on the phone.

**Fix (#3689):** the regex now only detects the phone and leaves the meaning to the builder, which reads language.
- **Detector:** it uses Q-846's own vocabulary, not widened, and tolerates spaces and dashes. It now matches the real prompt `Nokia c 2-01`, which the merged Q-846 regex never did.
- **Builder instruction:** the builder is told the likely meaning, the classic game from that phone in a retro 2D look, together with "if the request asks for something else, build what it asks".
- **User line:** it says only what is true under every reading: what was built and where it plays. It makes no claim about what the user meant and never says "cannot run", which was false for JioPhone and KaiOS.
- **Every lane gets the rule:** the architect, the fast lane, the writing sub-agents and the planner's goal.
- **Approved plans keep their notes:** an approved plan no longer rebuilds the build prompt from the bare request, which had dropped every note prepended to it.

**The lesson:** the first attempt tried to read intent with regexes over nine adversarial review rounds: origin vs target, refusals, owners, topics and Hinglish word order.
- It never converged. Every round found new phrasings.
- In round 5 it changed the classification of requests that name **no** phone, which is a regression on `main`.
- It was not merged. About 7M agent tokens went into it.
- The rule for next time: when the question is "what did the user mean", give the deterministic layer only what is true under every reading, and let the model decide the rest.

**Found while building:**
- **Q-975:** milestone mode replaces `buildPrompt` and drops every prepended note. The plan-approval sibling of the same bug is fixed here.

**Locks:**
- `tests/aPhoneTheAppCannotRunOnIsNamed.test.ts`: the real prompt is the fixture. Six guards, R1–R6, each reverted and seen to fail.
- `theRacingCarShowedItsHeadlights` 1c: the real prompt gets the 2D kit. The 3D guarantees are re-pinned on the same race without the phone.
- **Same day, harm-based review of the simple Q-868.** Four checks passed:
  - requests that name no phone behave as on `main` across 118,906 strings;
  - there are no new false positives;
  - the real prompt is detected;
  - all 551 related test files pass.

  One check failed, on the user line and the rule, and was fixed in the same PR:
  - **"any phone browser"** was false, because the Vite build targets modern browsers. The line now says "any **modern** phone or computer browser", and that an old keypad phone's own browser may not open it.
  - **The rule offered 3D while also saying "never three.js".** 3D is no longer offered.
  - **An edit turn got the rule.** An edit such as "add a Nokia 3310 pickup to my 3D city game" would have been told "never three.js". The rule now applies to a new build only.
  - **JioPhone, KaiOS and keypad phones are worded separately.** They are no longer told "the game that came on that phone".
  - **The plan-first planner now hears the rule.**

  The stale "📵 no web app runs there" comment is gone.
## 2026-10-12 — AUTOPSY `50378049`, Q-908: the one mechanism built to catch an abandoned kit was switched off by a prediction

Seventh PR from the BlockWorld autopsy (#3684 → Q-900…Q-904 · #3686 → Q-905 · #3688 → Q-911 · #3690 →
Q-906+Q-907 · #3693 → Q-909 · #3694 → Q-910).

**The defect.** The game kit seeded 24 files under `src/game/**`. The builder then wrote its own game
structure and used none of them, and `READINESS_WARNING` noted it had removed the only import of
`GameCanvas.tsx`. The orphan hand-back (Q-202, autopsy 3f959fde) exists for exactly that — a component
this build wrote that nothing imports — and it **named nothing**, because the turn was a project-mode
module and `starterExpected` was set.

🔑 **IT IS THE SAME CLASS AS Q-900, in the sibling I named in that PR's ledger and did not fix there.** A
plan-time PREDICTION disabled a mechanism, and the prediction was false.

**Two holes, and either one alone reproduces the report.**

1. **The carve-out outlived its premise.** It is excused because *"a component is wired in by a later
   module by design"* — and the thing that wires components in is the app's **ENTRY**. The moment THIS
   turn writes the entry, no later module is coming, so the premise is dead and the orphans are real.
   `wroteTheAppEntry(written)` is that fact: pure, local, read from the turn's own write set, with no new
   plumbing and no dependency on #3684's helper (deliberately — stacking is what I had to undo twice
   today).
   🔒 It is unreachable on an HONEST module turn, which is worth stating: a module that owns the entry
   makes `shellModuleFor` return null, so `starterExpected` is never set. It can only fire when the
   builder went OUT of its module's scope — exactly the reported build.
2. **Fixing (1) alone would have traded one problem for another.** The route's write set holds every kit
   file the seed wrote, so with the carve-out lifted the hand-back would have named OUR OWN untouched kit
   and told the model to wire in or delete 24 files it never wrote. `isPlatformSeededFile` is byte-exact
   and knows every kit version (Q-863) and every starter version (db07e0af), so platform files are
   excluded **inside `orphansToHandBack`** rather than at the call site — no caller can forget it. One
   edited byte makes a file the model's again, and nameable; a case proves both directions.

**Locked by** `tests/anAbandonedKitIsNotInvisible.test.ts` — 11 cases. **Reversion-proven twice:** restore
the unconditional carve-out → 3 fails · drop the platform-seeded exclusion → 1.

⚠️ **MY FIRST FIXTURE PROVED NOTHING, AND THE TEST SAID SO.** I handed it the whole real kit, and
`unreferencedComponents` is deliberately precise: it names nothing unless an entry exists AND every
relative import resolves to a file it was given. The kit's `Game.ts` imports seventeen files from four
OTHER recipes, so the graph refused and the answer was empty **for the wrong reason** — a green test would
have proved the opposite of what I wanted. The fixture is now the reported SHAPE with its imports closed,
and it uses the kit's REAL BYTES for `GameCanvas.tsx`, the one file the report names. **A fixture that
cannot fail is not evidence.**

⚠️ **AND I DELETED A CASE OF MY OWN THAT WAS FAKE.** One case asserted a local lambda standing in for the
old behaviour (`asItWas = (i) => i.starterExpected ? [] : […]`) — it could never fail whatever the code
did. The reversion probes do that job honestly; a test that exercises a copy of the code instead of the
code is worse than no test, because it reports confidence it has not earned.

⚠️ **AND THE Q-202 TEST THAT OWNS THIS CARVE-OUT FAILED — correctly, on a fixture that could not happen.**
Two of its cases passed a write set containing `src/App.tsx` while also setting `starterExpected: true`.
**The engine never produces that pair:** a module that owns an entry file makes `shellModuleFor` return
null, so `starterExpected` is never set for it. So those cases asserted the carve-out on a state that
cannot occur, and in doing so hid the state that DOES occur when a builder leaves its module's scope —
the reported build. Both now use a write set without the entry (the real state, still excused), and each
has gained a sibling asserting the new behaviour with the entry present. **One case became two, and the
pair is stronger than the one it replaces.**
## 2026-10-12 — AUTOPSY `50378049`, Q-910: "9 writes skipped" is not "9 files never compiled", and nothing recorded which

Sixth PR from the BlockWorld autopsy (#3684 → Q-900…Q-904 · #3686 → Q-905 · #3688 → Q-911 · #3690 →
Q-906+Q-907 · #3693 → Q-909).

**What the report said, verbatim:** *"9 TypeScript write(s) skipped before the compiler was ready — 9
because package.json had changed since the last install (a dependency may be missing until one runs)"*.
That reads as nine files that went unchecked.

**It may mean nothing of the kind.** `writeTypecheckCommand` runs `tsc --noEmit` over the WHOLE PROJECT,
not over the file just written — so ONE clean run after the last skip has already compiled every skipped
file. The two readings are opposite facts about the build:

| | what it cost |
|---|---|
| a later run succeeded | the skips cost a few seconds of lateness and nothing else |
| no later run succeeded | the end-of-build typecheck was those files' FIRST compile — the most expensive moment to find anything |

**Nothing recorded which, so nobody could tell.** That is the same gap `notReadyReasons` was added to
close one level up (build 46e2d74b: fourteen writes reported as *"still being installed"* when the tree
had only looked stale) — one sentence standing in for facts that mean different things.

🔒 **THE DEFERRAL ITSELF IS NOT THE DEFECT AND IS NOT TOUCHED.** Autopsy Sur Taal established that the
write-time check must never install and never wait: three such waits burned 90 s of a free build's clock
while the model sat holding a file. Making it wait again would trade this report's item for that one.
What is fixed is what the report SAYS about the skips — the fourth rule's fifth step.

**The fix.** `WriteTypecheckStats.cleanRunCoveredSkips` — `true` when a clean run followed the last skip,
`false` when none did, `null`/absent when the question was never asked (never a silent "no"). Order is
the whole answer: a skip sets it back to `false`, because a clean run BEFORE the skip compiled a project
that did not yet hold these files; only a clean run after it may set `true`, and only when something was
actually skipped. The report then says either *"a later check compiled the whole project, so those files
were covered, just later than they should have been"* or *"no check succeeded after them, so the
end-of-build typecheck was their first compile"*.

**Locked by** `tests/aSkippedCheckIsNotAnUncheckedFile.test.ts` — 10 cases, including the premise itself
(the command carries no per-file argument, so a project-wide run really does cover the skips), both new
sentences, the absent case saying nothing extra, and a recorder guard asserting the write sits inside the
CLEAN-RUN branch — a compiler that never ran covers nothing (autopsy 12c642ed's class). **Reversion-proven
three ways:** stop putting the question back on a skip → 1 fail · stop answering it on a clean run → 1 ·
never print the sentence → 2.

⚠️ **A GUARD OF MINE MEASURED THE WRONG THING, and the fix is the repo's own rule.** The recorder case
first looked back 260 characters for the enclosing branch and failed on the `neverRan` branch that
legitimately sits just above. **A byte window measures distance; the claim was about NESTING.** This repo
has paid for byte-window guards before (`slice(0, 6000)`), and the rule is to anchor on syntax — it now
asserts that nothing intervenes between `if (errors.length === 0) {` and the write, and that the branch
has not closed before it.

⚠️ **AND AN EXISTING GUARD BROKE ON ITS ANCHOR, EXACTLY THE SAME WAY** —
`tests/aCompilerThatNeverRanIsNotClean.test.ts` pinned the literal one-liner
`if (errors.length === 0) s.cleanRuns += 1;`, which became a BLOCK when that branch gained the Q-910
line. **Found by the full suite, not by me**, and the invariant it protects was never in danger: the
`if (neverRan) { s.notRunRuns += 1; return ''; }` branch still returns before the clean count, so a
compiler that never ran can never set `cleanRunCoveredSkips`. Re-anchored on the branch opener, which
survives a statement being added and still breaks on a REORDERING — proven by letting the never-ran
branch fall through and watching it fail. Its own `-1` hole is closed in the same edit (only one of its
three anchors was asserted present, so a rename would have read as a reordering).

**That is three anchor re-pins in this autopsy** (`theCommitMessageWasNotADevServer`, my own ordering
case in `aKitTypeIsNotGuessed`, and this one), and the lesson is one sentence: **a guard that pins a
LINE breaks when the line grows; a guard that pins the SYNTAX it is really about does not.** The
underlying invariants were correct every time — only the instruments were brittle.

### 🔸 Q-914 advanced, not fixed — what the evidence actually supports

Investigated in the same session and recorded rather than guessed:
- **The rule is already in the prompt, unconditionally.** `architectSystemPrompt` carries *"Define CSS
  variables on :root for a real palette"* with no game carve-out, so the build did receive it. This is
  not a missing instruction.
- **The scanner is not inflating the count.** `DesignLinter.allColors` matches `/#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b/`
  only — `0x`-form three.js material colours are NOT counted, so the 45 are real CSS-shaped colours.
- **The finding needs BOTH conditions:** `allColors.length > 8 && !hasTokens`. It fired, so the app had
  **no token layer at all** — the finding is true, not a false positive.

So Q-914 is a prompt-ADHERENCE failure on a game's UI panels, and the honest fix is a decision, not a
one-liner: mandate tokens for a game's UI in the kit's own contract (cheap, preventive), or add a pass
that rewrites them (risky — a voxel game's block colours are DATA, not theme, and a rewriter cannot tell
them apart from `Hud.tsx`'s). It stays OPEN with this analysis, and what would settle it is the built
app's own files from one game report.
## 2026-10-12 — AUTOPSY `50378049`, Q-909: the builder had to reverse-engineer a file WE wrote

Fifth PR from the BlockWorld autopsy (#3684 → Q-900…Q-904 · #3686 → Q-905 · #3688 → Q-911 · #3690 →
Q-906+Q-907).

**The defect.** NavBharatAI seeded its game kit before the builder's first call, and the handoff told it
exactly which functions to call — `<GameCanvas>`, `ctx.follow(vehicle)`, `driveVehicle(…)` — with a
compiling example. **What it never said was what `ctx` IS.** The example touches three of
`GameContext`'s nine members, so for the rest the model guessed, and guessed our PRIVATE fields:

| it reached for | what that actually is |
|---|---|
| `ctx.canvas` | `private readonly canvas` on `Game` — never on the context |
| `ctx.followTarget` | `private followTarget` — the state behind `ctx.follow()` |
| `ctx.crosshairTarget` | nothing at all |
| `TouchButton` as a string | `{ action: string; label: string }` |

Cost in that one build: **four `read_file` slices of `Game.ts` and two of `touchControls.ts`** — the
model reverse-engineering a file we wrote — and the repeated-step nudges that followed.

🔑 **The fix is the one this repo already uses for the same problem.** Project Mode freezes a per-module
CONTRACT precisely so a later turn imports *"against these EXACT names"* instead of guessing. A seeded
kit is the same situation — code the builder must use and did not write — and it had no contract.
`src/server/lib/kitTypeContract.ts` builds one, and the shell's instructions carry it.

🔒 **EXTRACTED FROM THE EMITTED SOURCE, NEVER HAND-WRITTEN.** A hand-kept copy of a type is the drift
this repo has paid for repeatedly (four `safeRelPath`s, two complex-app detectors, five hardcoded model
ids). `extractExportedDeclaration` reads the declaration out of the very file the recipe writes —
brace-balanced, comments stripped — so renaming a member updates the contract in the same commit, by
construction. A **census** asserts that every member of the emitted `GameContext` appears in the block
the builder reads, so the contract cannot silently fall behind the type.

🔒 **PLACEMENT IS PART OF THE FIX.** `gameKitSeed.compactRecipeResult` clips a recipe's instructions at
`HANDOFF_RECIPE_CHARS` (6,000), so a contract at the bottom is a contract the builder may never see. It
goes at the TOP, above the example, and two cases pin that — one of them by running the real
`compactRecipeResult` and asserting the heading's index is below the clip.

**Locked by** `tests/aKitTypeIsNotGuessed.test.ts` — 12 cases on the REAL emitted kit, including the
census, the three names the reported build guessed (asserted NOT to be members, so the contract's *"if a
name is not here, the kit does not have it"* is true), and the extractor's refusals. **Reversion-proven
three ways:** drop the contract → 2 fails · move it to the bottom → 1 · narrow the covered names so the
contract falls behind the type → 2 (this is the drift probe, and it is the important one).

⚠️ **A HOLE IN MY OWN TEST, found by probing it.** With the contract removed, the ordering case PASSED —
`indexOf` returned `-1`, and `-1 < 2000` is true. That is the exact *"-1 < -1 arithmetic"* trap
`importPreviewOrdering.test.ts` warns about, and I walked into it one file away from the warning. Both
anchors are now asserted `> 0` before they are compared, and the reason is written in the case. **An
ordering assertion is only as good as its anchors.**

**🔸 Q-912 is NOT claimed by this.** The report's three *"repeated step that isn't making progress"*
nudges have at least two causes: the repeated `read_file` of our own kit, which this removes, and a LOOP
GUARD on `console_errors`, which is a different thing. Calling Q-912 resolved because its biggest cause
is gone would be the "fixed the instance, not the class" mistake this ledger exists to prevent. It stays
OPEN, and the next report with a seeded game says whether the read loop is gone.
## 2026-10-12 — NATIVE FEEL, ROUND 3: round 1 fixed the reader and left the source — fourteen viewports, not one with the token

The admin's standing instruction (*"navbharatai jo app banaye aur navbharatai khud dono ko real netiv app
feel aye aisa banao! aur bhi jyada micro polish karo"*). Rounds 1 (#3669) and 2 (#3671) are merged.

### Measured first, and three of four candidates were already done

Before adding anything, the obvious round-3 ideas were checked against the code rather than assumed:

| candidate | state |
|---|---|
| iOS input zoom (<16px focus zoom) | ✅ already handled, BOTH sides (`nativeFeel.ts:158`, `index.css:468`) |
| tap highlight, overscroll, touch-action, user-select | ✅ round 1 |
| safe-area variables, Apple meta tags | ✅ round 1 |
| **our own app's `100vh`** | ✅ **already correct** — its three `index.css` sites use the `100vh` → `100dvh` fallback pattern, with the reasons written down |

So the honest answer for NavBharatAI itself was *nothing to fix*, and saying that beats churn. **Both real
gaps were on the apps-we-build side.**

### 🔴 GAP 1 — round 1 fixed the READER and left the SOURCE

`withViewportFitCover` PATCHES a user's `index.html` at build time, so an AgentV3 build gets
`viewport-fit=cover` and its `env(safe-area-inset-*)` stops reading 0px. Measured afterwards: **not one
of the fourteen viewport tags in the scaffold templates carried the token.** Thirteen provider templates
(`ViteReactProviderContents`, `Vue`, `Svelte`, `SvelteKit`, `Astro`×2, `Angular`, `Preact`, `Solid`,
`Lit`, `Vanilla`, `Remix`, `Alpine`, `Static`) each hand-wrote their own string — so there was nowhere to
add it once, and **any lane that does not pass through `appDefaults` shipped the exact defect round 1 was
written for.**

🔑 **This repo's headline class, in its own words:** an instance fixed at one reader, the source left
alone, and the siblings never hunted. `APP_VIEWPORT_CONTENT` / `APP_VIEWPORT_META` now live in
`nativeFeel.ts` beside the reason, and the templates import them. `withViewportFitCover` stays as defence
in depth: it returns a document untouched once the token is present, so a correct template makes it a
no-op instead of a rescue — a case asserts both directions.

🔒 No `maximum-scale` / `user-scalable=no`: pinch-zoom is an accessibility right and blocking it fails a
store review. The native feel comes from the safe area, not from forbidding zoom.

🔒 **What is deliberately OUT, with the reason in the test** — the email generator (mail clients ignore
`viewport-fit` and some choke on unknown tokens) and the three preview runtimes (they RENDER an app, they
do not ship one; changing them changes what we show, not what the user gets). Recorded so the exclusion
is a decision rather than an oversight, and so nobody "finishes the job" by adding the token to an email.

### 🔴 GAP 2 — a full-height app must end where the SCREEN ends

`100vh` on a phone is the LARGE viewport: it includes the collapsing address bar, so a `height: 100vh`
layout is cut off by exactly the toolbar height and the page scrolls when it should not. That is the
clearest "web page, not app" tell left once the safe area is handled, and the built-app baseline had
**no `dvh` at all**. Added: `--app-height` (plain `100vh` first, then `@supports (height: 100dvh)`), an
`html` min-height with the same two-line pattern, and a build-rule line that NAMES the variable instead
of merely forbidding `100vh` — round 2's lesson that a rule naming no primitive is aspirational.

### Proof

`tests/aViewportEveryLaneWrites.test.ts` — **38 cases**. It GENERATES every one of the thirteen
frameworks and reads the document the provider really emits, so the token is proven in the output, not in
the diff. Plus a **CENSUS**: no file in the template directory may hand-write a viewport, every user of
the constant must import it, and the out-of-scope list is pinned with its reasons.

**Reversion-proven three ways:** drop the token from the shared constant → **15 fails** · let one
template hand-write its viewport again → **3** · remove the `dvh` override → **1**.

### ⚠️ Three mistakes of mine, all caught by a guard

- **The backtick trap, a THIRD time in one session** (#3671, #3693, here) — a CSS comment inside
  `NATIVE_FEEL_CSS`, which is a TS template literal. `tsc` passed and the TEST LOADER caught it (`oxc`
  parse error). The file now says in its own text that it may not contain backticks.
- **My filter could return nothing, and did.** `htmlOf` missed `.astro` entirely, so the astro case
  asserted against an empty string — a case that fails for the wrong reason is one edit away from a case
  that PASSES for the wrong reason. Every case now asserts the document is non-empty first.
- **A blanket assertion was wrong.** `expect(html).not.toContain('${')` failed on Remix's `root.tsx`,
  which is generated code that legitimately contains its own template literals. It now asserts the
  specific literal cannot ship — the precise claim instead of the broad one.

### ⚠️ And two EXISTING guards caught consequences I had not thought of

- **`aBuiltAppFeelsNative`'s "chooses no colour" rule read `#3671` as a hex colour.** Writing the PR
  references as a hash plus four hex digits inside the stylesheet matched its
  `/#[0-9a-f]{3,8}\b/i` exactly. **The guard was right** — and notably STRONGER than the colour check I
  wrote in my own new test, which only extracts `background`/`color`/`border-color` declarations and
  would never have seen a bare hex. The comment now says both of its own rules (no backticks, no hash
  before a number) so the next editor does not rediscover either.
- **`anOlderStarterIsStillOurs` failed because I changed what the templates write.** That census (autopsy
  `db07e0af`) requires every file a template emits TODAY to be in the seed history — which is what lets
  `isPlatformSeededFile` recognise an untouched starter as OURS. Changing fourteen viewport tags without
  it would have made every new `index.html` read as the USER's code: the quality lint would grade our own
  starter, and Q-908's brand-new platform-seeded exclusion would stop recognising it. **A genuine
  fix-A-create-X, caught by a guard another session built.** Regenerated: 76 starter paths · 35 golden
  paths · 455 versions, 55 new.

## 2026-10-13 — AUTOPSY `50378049`: THE LAST THREE. Q-912, Q-913, Q-914 — and I was wrong to have held them

The admin, verbatim: *"maine kaha tha: build report ki sabhi problem ko ek ek kar ke solve karna hai, dna
level par, jab tak sabhi ke root cause fix na ho jaye tab tak rukna nahi hai! toh sab ho gaya??"*

**The honest answer was NO** — 12 of 15, with three held as "needs a decision / needs evidence". That was
wrong. Each of the three had a real root cause reachable from the code, and digging found it in every
case. What follows is what was actually there.

### 🔴 Q-914 — the app was graded for a token system nobody asked it for

`DESIGN_CONSISTENCY 60/100`, *"45 hardcoded colours and no CSS variables"*, **unresolved**. Checked one
layer at a time: the rule IS in the prompt unconditionally; the scanner is honest (`#rrggbb` only, so a
three.js `0x…` colour is never counted); the finding needs `> 8 colours` AND `!hasTokens` and it fired,
so the app really had no token layer. **The finding was true.**

🔑 So the engine MEASURED it, SCORED it, told the USER — and **never once asked the MODEL to fix it.**
`hardcoded-colors` lives in `WHOLE_APP_VIOLATIONS`, correctly kept out of the per-file write-time note
because it is a whole-app judgement — and then it reached no hand-back either. **A finding with nowhere
to go is a grade, not a fix.**

It belongs in the end-of-turn hand-back by that module's OWN rule, written there in advance: *"a hand-back
is for what only a model can JUDGE … never for arithmetic with one answer."* Which literals are the same
semantic colour, and what to call them, is exactly that — unlike `round(v / 4) * 4`, which is why spacing
was moved OUT of the hand-back into `spacingSnap.ts` (autopsy 536c8189).

🔑 **AND THE DATA WAS ALREADY IN HAND AND THROWN AWAY.** `undefinedClassesNow` already calls
`lintBuiltApp(project)` for its a11y half; that one result carries `design.stats.hasTokens` and a counted
`hardcoded-colors` with its worst files, and every bit but a11y was discarded. One lint, read twice — no
second pass, no extra reads. Bounded to ONE stylesheet edit, fired only when the app has NO tokens
whatsoever (never on partial adoption), and never handed to a sub-agent (Q-066's rule, same as `orphans`).

### 🔴 Q-913 — the measurement existed; nothing said it had not run

The dark screen's only account in the report was the MODEL's prose — *"normal for a sandbox game, players
can move and dig to daylight"*. **The engine's own measurement for exactly that already existed:**
`scorePlaytest`'s `runs` dimension reads the brightness SPREAD of a 48×27 sample (the standard deviation
of luminance, zero for any flat colour) and scores **0** — *"The game screen is blank or a single colour"*.

It never ran, because the preview address had been discarded (Q-900). **And nothing said so.** The route's
playtest gate is one long `if (…)` **with no `else`**, so a canvas game the route could not play was
SILENTLY skipped — while `playtestNotRunVerdict` promises, in its own words, *"one sentence for every way
it is reached (the runner's own answer, and the route's timeout or crash)"*. The THIRD way — the route
never calling it — had no sentence.

`playtestSkipReason` is that sentence, and it keeps the two facts apart: a project with no canvas game, an
import turn, a stopped build, a failed build and the kill switch are NOT APPLICABLE and stay silent; a
canvas game with no preview address, a module turn awaiting its shell, no command channel or no time left
is COULD NOT LOOK and gets the open warning that already existed.

🔒 **I did NOT add a second dark-screen detector**, and that was deliberate: `browseUrl` returns no pixels,
so a check there would have been a weaker copy of a tested one — the drifted-copy class this repo has paid
for four times.

### 🔴 Q-912 — a check after a fix is a new question, not a repeat

The report's `LOOP GUARD` fired on `console_errors`. That call reads the LIVE app's console, so after an
edit it is a **new question with the same spelling** — check, fix, check again. The guard counted it as a
non-progressing repeat, nagged, and because `console_errors` is in `PROBE_TOOLS` it would eventually have
**refused the model's only way of telling whether its own fix had worked.**

🔑 This module already makes the argument one tool over: `bash` is excluded because a repeated
`tsc --noEmit` *"looks identical to a loop and is usually a build legitimately converging — check, fix,
check again"*. `console_errors`, `screenshot`, `evaluate` and `browser_action` have the same shape and
were bannable anyway.

🔒 **The discriminator is not the TOOL, it is whether anything CHANGED.** A signature's count now resets
when the build has mutated since that signature was last seen. The original autopsy's loop — six identical
`grep`s with nothing written between them — is **still caught**, because nothing mutated during it; a case
proves that, and another proves a ban must be earned again after a change.

⚠️ **AND MY FIRST VERSION RE-BROKE Q-738 WITHIN THE HOUR.** It counted every `bash` as a mutation, so the
SEVEN empty `bash` calls of autopsy `d0b2fcd6` each reset the count: FINAL was never reached,
`MAX_NO_OP_TURNS_AFTER_FINAL` never applied, and a run doing nothing forever would never end.
`tests/aRunThatOnlyDoesNothingEnds` caught it immediately. `isEmptyCommandCall` already recognised that
call — the dispatcher refuses it before the shell — so an empty command no longer counts as a change, and
a reversion probe shows BOTH that test and mine failing when it does.

### Proof

Three new files, 40 cases: `anAppGradedForTokensItNeverGot` (13) · `aGameNobodyPlayedSaysSo` (15) ·
`aCheckAfterAFixIsANewQuestion` (12). **Reversion-proven nine ways**, three per item.

⚠️ **The SERVER typecheck caught one the frontend one missed:** `undefinedClassesNow`'s inline return type
did not declare `noTokens`, so the runner's read of it would not compile. Both typechecks are in the gate
for exactly this, and only one of them saw it.

⚠️ **AND THREE MORE GUARDS BROKE ON THEIR ANCHORS — the sixth, seventh and eighth of this autopsy.** All
three pinned a field's POSITION in an argument list (`'a11y: style.a11y, orphans: style.orphans,
resumesUsed: styleResumes'`; a full `styleResumeNote(...)` call; the one-liner
`a11yHandBack(lintBuiltApp(project))`), so inserting a fifth hand-back part broke them without touching
anything they protect. Each now asserts its intent — the architect's call carries the orphans and the
specialist's does not; both runners pass the a11y count; the lint is taken exactly once — and each was
re-probed to prove it still fails on a REAL break (drop the a11y field: fails; lint twice: fails).

🔑 **Eight anchor re-pins in one autopsy is itself a finding, and the lesson is one line:** a guard that
pins a LINE, a BYTE WINDOW, or a field's POSITION breaks when the code around it grows; a guard that pins
the SYNTAX or the RELATIONSHIP it is really about does not. Every one of the eight underlying invariants
was correct — only the instruments were brittle. `tests/theQueueQ002`'s title (*"from the same read"*) is
now MORE true than when it was written, which is the shape a good re-anchor takes.

### The one sentence worth keeping from this autopsy

**Three of the fifteen were the same mistake wearing different clothes: a PREDICTION allowed to outrank
an OBSERVATION.** Q-900 (the plan said nothing was openable, so a live address was discarded), Q-906/907
(the project score said the app was finished, so the model was told to stop ten steps in), Q-908 (the plan
said a later module would wire the components in, so an abandoned kit stayed invisible). Each fix is the
same shape — the prediction yields to what actually happened — and that is the missing subsystem this
report exposed.

**Four more were the same mistake one level up: a finding with nowhere to go.** Q-901 and Q-910 (the report
said something untrue, or said something true that read as worse than it was), Q-913 (a measurement that
never ran and nothing said so), Q-914 (a grade the model was never asked to act on). A measurement nobody
is accountable to is decoration.

**And the engine's own tests were the most reliable reviewer in the room.** Eight guards broke on brittle
anchors, and every one of the eight invariants underneath was correct; three existing tests caught real

## 2026-10-13 — Q-975: a milestone build keeps its notes, and every lane builds the milestone

**Why this one.** While #3698 ran CI, the queue had one actionable, unclaimed code row: Q-975. The BlockWorld rows
(Q-905…Q-911) were all merged by another session's PRs, which also own closing them. Q-912/Q-913 have no PR and no
report data in the repo. Q-914 waits on a decision.

**Correction first.** The row said milestone mode was flag-gated and not user-visible. It is not: `AGENTV3_MEGA_ROADMAP`
has been ON by default since 2026-08-14 and is only a kill switch. Every milestone build (39e982bd, 728a402d were two)
ran with the defect.

**The class:** a reader of "what this build is building" that assembles the request for itself. Three were found:
- **The builder.** `buildPrompt = step1.buildPrompt + …` replaced the whole prompt and threw away every note prepended
  above the user's words. `milestoneBuildPrompt` (megaRoadmap.ts) now replaces only the user's words — every note is a
  prepend, so they are the suffix — keeps the notes, adds one line saying a whole-app note does not widen the milestone,
  and still restates the hard constraints (681bd91b). If the request can ever not be separated, `MILESTONE_NOTES_DROPPED`
  says so as a warning.
- **The two fast lanes.** On a milestone build they were handed the WHOLE message, so a fast lane planned the entire app
  while the builder built milestone 1. And each lane added its own pick of the notes: the one-shot got two of five (no
  classic-phone rule, no one-file rule, no pasted checklist) from the bare words without the attachment. **So #3689's
  claim that the Q-868 classic-phone rule "reaches every lane" missed the one-shot.** Now there is ONE `fastLaneRequest`
  for both lanes.
- **The writing specialist.** Its `userRequest` was the whole message too; on a milestone build it is now the milestone.

**Locked:** `tests/aMilestoneKeepsItsNotes.test.ts` (14). It checks the behaviour, plus a census: every note before the
swap is a prepend, no later `buildPrompt =` starts from a bare request, and both lanes pass `fastLaneRequest`. Five
reversions each fail it (wholesale swap, one-shot composing its own, helper dropping notes, an append before the swap,
specialist given the whole message). Ten older source guards were updated to the one-request shape, with their intent
kept (each note still reaches each lane).

**After #3698 merged (2026-10-13), and Q-979 opened.** On top of #3692, `typecheck:server` failed with TS2563 in the
`/build` handler: TypeScript's control-flow limit. The merging session fixed #3698's share while landing it (the
leftover-net guard moved into `applyLeftoverNetAfterBuild`). This PR, rebuilt on that `main`, adds zero branches to the
handler: the milestone's dropped-notes record lives in `milestoneBuildPrompt`, "not a milestone" is a `null` that
`milestoneLaneRequest` handles, and the existing stay record moved into `recordReasoningStays` (FastLaneBudget) for
headroom. Each has a behaviour test, reversion-proven. The handler being at the limit is a defect in its own right —
any session's next `if` there turns CI red — so it is now **Q-979** (OPEN, unowned), with a plan to make headroom one
module at a time. Rows Q-926, Q-976, Q-977 and Q-978 closed (merged in #3698).

## 2026-10-13 — Q-1038: a frame-driven simulation sampled by a stopwatch

The flake that gated report 9c612cdb's PR and then #3703. The row's diagnosis was right about the class
and wrong about the place, and the difference only showed up because the fix was **measured under load
instead of reasoned about**.

**What the row said to fix:** the steering leg — `hold(page, ['ArrowLeft','KeyA'], 500)` and the
`waitForTimeout(400)` interval the turn is read across. True, and insufficient: with that leg frame-gated
the test **still failed** under three CPU hogs.

**Where it actually lives:** the ACCELERATOR probe's `waitForTimeout(550)`. `out.scene` — `moved`,
`follows`, `ahead`, `looks` — is read across that one interval, and *both* `sceneVerdict` fields sit
behind its `moved >= 0.2` guard. So a page starved there nulls the camera reading and, through the guard,
the steering reading as well. Frame-gating the steering leg could never have been enough, and the row
could not have known: it reasoned from the symptom's name ("mirrored: null") to the probe that computes
`turn`.

🧬 **It is Q-869's class, in the place that fix did not reach.** Q-869 removed exactly this dependence
from the PIXEL verdicts — a page a loaded machine stops drawing shows the same picture whatever the car
does, so those looks record `gasLateFrames` and are believed only when the page was drawing. The scene
probes, in the same file, kept their stopwatch. The instance was fixed; the class was not.

**The fix, both halves:** both windows wait for DRAWN frames (`waitFrames`, with a wall-clock cap so a
dead raf loop cannot hang the probe); the WEAKEST leg sets `probeFrames`, because one starved interval is
enough to null a reading; and a starved probe is NAMED — *"page starved: 3 frames in 2500 ms"* — instead
of returning a null that reads identically to the real finding "this game does not steer". That is
`playtestNotRunVerdict`'s own stated principle one level down: **a check that could not look is not a
check that passed.** It changes no score: the probe failing to look is our instrument's problem, not the
app's, exactly as the not-run warning says.

**Evidence, because "it should be fine now" is not evidence:** 6/6 unloaded; 3/3 on the previously-failing
case under three CPU hogs (load 3.5 on 4 cores) — the same conditions under which the partial fix failed.

🔴 **Bugs this change caught in itself, all worth recording as classes:**

1. **A bare TypeScript constant inside the browser script.** The accelerator fix was first written
   `waitFrames(page, PROBE_MIN_FRAMES, PROBE_CAP_MS)` — no `${…}`. Inside the template literal that is
   not the constant, it is an identifier the BROWSER must resolve, and it would have thrown a
   ReferenceError in the accelerator step, left `out.scene` unset, and nulled every scene verdict —
   turning an intermittent flake into a permanent one. **It survived a full typecheck**, because a
   template literal's contents are text, and no browser test had run since that edit. Only a source
   assertion noticed. Guarded now.
2. **An unescaped backtick in a script comment ends the template literal** — three times in this one
   change. The compiler does catch it, but TS1005 points at the next line that fails to parse, twenty
   lines past the cause. The guard names the line; it is a diagnostics fix, not a new safety net, and
   that is what its comment says rather than overclaiming it.

🔴 **AND THEN THE MEASUREMENT SAID THE ROW'S PRESCRIBED FIX WAS HARMFUL.** The row said to *"hold LEFT
until N rendered frames … with a wall-clock cap"*. That was built — and it made things worse, twice over:

1. Waiting for frames ALONE is SHORTER than the interval it replaced on a fast machine: twelve frames is
   about 200 ms against 550 ms, so `out.gas` saw less change, fell under the still threshold, and the gas
   optical-flow sample was never taken. Adding the original duration back as a floor fixed that.
2. But the floor exposed the real objection. On a loaded machine the hold stretched to as much as
   2500 ms — and **the car does not politely wait.** It drives four times further: into a wall, off the
   road, or past the turn the next sample meant to read. Under three CPU hogs,
   `aRacingGameIsStartedAndDriven` passed **7/7 twice on main** and failed **1 then 3** on that branch.
   Gathering more frames CHANGED WHAT THERE WAS TO MEASURE.

🧬 **So the fix became what Q-869 ACTUALLY did, rather than what it looked like it did.** Q-869 did not
make the pixel looks longer. It RECORDED how many frames the page drew during them and refused to believe
a verdict taken while the page was not drawing. The intervals here keep their exact original lengths —
550 ms and 400 ms, untouched — the frames drawn in them are counted, and a reading taken across too few
is reported as starved instead of returned as a null that reads exactly like the real finding "this game
does not steer". After the rework: **7/7 twice under the same load**, matching main.

⚠️ **The lesson is not "the row was wrong", it is that a prescribed fix on a SIMULATION needs measuring
before it is believed.** The row's author reasoned correctly from the symptom and could not have known
that lengthening a hold moves the car; only running it under load showed that. The row's second half —
*print "page starved" instead of a silent null* — was right all along, and is the whole fix now.

**Proof.** 14 tests (`tests/aStarvedPageIsSaidNotGuessed.test.ts`), the two real-browser suites green together (32/32), and the regression case 7/7 twice under three CPU hogs. The rejected design is asserted GONE, not merely unused, so it cannot creep back as an optimisation. Two of those
reversions found holes in the lock itself: removing the accelerator frame-gate left all thirteen other
tests green, and the bare-constant bug was invisible until a source assertion existed. A reversion that
passes is the test telling you it is not watching.

## 2026-10-13 — Q-1040/Q-1041/Q-1042: the deep bug hunt is offered, not assumed

Admin instruction, verbatim: *"helper, verifier jo app banne ke bad last me check karta hai, ko optional
kar do"* — a ❓ question in the chat, Yes runs the helper that already exists, No means the build is
complete as it stands.

**The investigation came first, and its result changed the framing.** Nine searches (60 commits, the
user-facing strings, the flags, filenames, the queue, `PROGRESS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/claude/`,
Hindi/Hinglish phrasings, 12 open and recent PRs, all 1,435 remote branches) found no trace of this
feature and **no record of the instruction anywhere** — reported to the admin as *"I could not find it"*,
never as "it does not exist", because only one of those two is a verified claim.

What the search DID find is the thing that mattered: **the helper is not a free check being made paid.
It is a PAID check being made optional.** The route's own comment beside the reviewer call records the
size, autopsy b6f88a72: *"40 calls, 523,374 input tokens = 34.4% of the build, `responseChars: 0` on
every one, and then no verdict at all — all of it billed at ×4"*. The user already paid for that, on
every build, silently. The admin's own words — the real build costs x, the helper takes 4x — are
corroborated by the code. So this change does not introduce a charge; it shows an existing one to the
person paying it.

**What stays free, and why that is the point.** The deterministic end-of-build checks — the tsc gate,
lint, readiness, the playtest, the fake-feature scan, the journeys, the app's own tests — spend no model
tokens and sit in no billing phase. They are the EVIDENCE that the app was built at all, which the
second absolute rule requires, so putting them behind a payment would make a free build mean "it
probably works". They are untouched.

**Three admin decisions, implemented as given.** (1) No amount on the button — and that is the only
honest option anyway: a token-metered cost has no true number before it runs, so a figure there would be
a fabricated quote. (2) A "no" is scoped to ONE build, implemented by storing *nothing* — the offer is
turn-local, so there is nothing to forget and nothing to reset. (3) Free and gift credits pay for it.

🔴 **One admin instruction was NOT followed, and raised instead (third absolute rule).** The admin asked
for the question in the user's language. `narrationCatalogue.ts` carries the admin's own 2026-08-11 rule
— a status line is the PLATFORM speaking, not the AI, and an earlier Hindi table there was removed as
wrong and unmaintainable ("22 hand-written translations per line") — and on 2026-09-14 the admin saw a
voice-chat **price** in Devanagari and asked *"south india wale kaise padhenge isko??"*, superseding
three modules' "user's language" behaviour. This offer IS a price. Building it translated would
re-create exactly what they stopped, so it is professional English and the admin was told, with the
reasoning, rather than quietly obeyed.

🔴 **Q-979's ceiling was hit live, by this feature.** The first version put its `let`, its nested `if`s
and its two `try`s inline in the `/build` handler, and `tsc` answered **TS2563: the containing function
or module body is too large for control flow analysis** — the exact row draft #3700 owns. Rather than
touch that row (it is taken), the whole flow moved into `optionalBugHunt.ts` with its effects injected
(`ask` / `wait` / `say` / `record`), leaving the handler at ONE call and one `await`. A source guard
asserts no branch, no `let` and no second `await` inside it, and says why: in that handler, the cost of
a branch is the whole file. This is the better design regardless — every branch is now unit-testable
without a server, a user or a clock.

**Q-1041, found while building.** `permission_request` carried the whole question as one string, which
the tray printed as a bold title with an empty detail line and two *fixed* buttons. That is why
`startOfferText` has to spell "Approve = … Deny = …" inside its own sentence — the buttons could not be
labelled — and why a gate that builds nothing still offered to "Approve & build". The event gained four
optional fields, threaded through to the tray; **a gate that names none of them renders byte-for-byte as
before**, which a test asserts on the fallbacks themselves.

**Q-1042, the honest leftover.** The admin's instinct — run the helper on the cheap tier — is the actual
cure; hiding the price treats the symptom. Recorded as an open row with what it needs: the cheap rung
must be measured against the Sonnet judge before it becomes the default, because a cheaper hunt that
misses real bugs is worse than an honest "not run".

**Proof.** `tests/aBugHuntIsOfferedNotAssumed.test.ts`, 24 tests. Eight reversions, each failing the
right test: silence counted as consent; a declined hunt reported as passed; a made-up rupee figure on
the button; the fail-open flipped to fail-closed; the kill switch turning the review off instead of the
ask; the wait bypassing `waitForUser` (the one door, autopsy 1219c639); the button offering to "build"
again; and the tray ignoring a gate's own labels. The 130 tests across every module this touched
(`whatTheUserMustDo`, `theTrayKnowsWhatIsNotConnected`, `everyPopupClearsTheChrome`, `buildNeeds`) pass
unchanged.
## 2026-10-13 — Q-1026 + Q-1033: two copies of one truth, where only one of them is the truth

Two rows from build report 9c612cdb, closed together because they are ONE class — the fourth absolute
rule's centralisation class, the same shape as the four drifted `safeRelPath` copies that became
`workspacePath.ts` and the five hardcoded model ids that became `visionModels.ts`.

**Q-1026 — the contract's home.** Two facts about the contract module were each written twice. The
relative import specifier existed as `importSpecifierFor` in `contractRenames.ts` and
`contractImportSpecifier` in `SimpleBuilder.ts`, byte-identical bodies. That pair is the lesser half.
The real defect was the other pair: the WRITER decided where the contract goes (`contractFilePath`)
while the HEALERS searched a hand-kept list (`CONTRACT_PATH_CANDIDATES`). Nothing made them agree.
Move the contract to a third location in the writer — `app/types.ts` for a Next project — and the
healers find no contract, report no renames, and hand every TS2749 they exist to fix back to the
model. **And no test fails**, because the list is still internally consistent; it is simply no longer
about reality. That is the quiet kind of drift: not a wrong value, a true value about the wrong world.

The fix is `src/server/AgentV3/contractLocation.ts`, and it is STRUCTURAL rather than a merge of the
two copies: the candidate list is derived from the very two constants `contractFilePath` returns, so a
new location cannot enter the writer without appearing in the search. `ToolDispatcher` takes the
candidates from that one home rather than through `contractRenames` — a re-export chain would have put
two definition-looking lines back under `grep`, which is how the next session re-derives the wrong
source of truth.

**Q-1033 — a bill has one rule.** The money predicate `(paid-public OR credit-gate) AND not
free-listed` was written SIX times in `routes/agentv3.ts`: the affordability gate, the cheap-floor
chain, the watchdog's billing label, the watchdog's wallet debit, the live ₹ figure and the settle. It
has already been widened once — the credit gate was OR-ed in on 2026-07-10 — so this is not a
hypothetical: the next widening that reaches five of the six leaves the sixth charging, or not
charging, by a rule nobody chose. A money predicate is the last place a copy may drift. Now one
`billingAppliesTo()` in `featureFlag.ts`.

🔴 **What was deliberately NOT done, and why it matters more than what was.** The live figure's call
site reads `!!userId && <predicate>`. Folding that `!!userId` into the shared helper would have given
a tidier signature and silently stopped charging the five sites that never had it — fixing problem A
while creating problem X, which the 2026-09-13 rule forbids outright. The helper answers "is billing
on for them", never "is there someone to bill", and a test asserts the helper's body contains no
`!!userId` so the tidier version cannot arrive later as a cleanup.

**The guard that was itself the bug's shelter.** `theBuildShowsWhatItCostsSoFar` had a source guard
asserting the live figure used "the settle's own predicate, word for word". Its intent was right and
its mechanism was exactly why six copies could sit in one file and still read as one rule: it pinned
the TEXT. It now asserts both readings call the function, and that no copy of the text survives.

**Proof.** `tests/aContractHasOneHomeAndABillHasOneRule.test.ts`, 9 tests. The census WALKS the engine
tree rather than reading a list of files to check — a hand-kept list of files is the same drift class
the test exists to end — with vacuity guards (the walk must reach `SimpleBuilder.ts` and
`contractRenames.ts`, and find more than fifty sources) so a narrowed walk cannot pass green. Nine
reversions, each failing the right test and nothing else: a second specifier implementation under
another name, a dead candidate the writer can never produce, the writer moving away from the search
(the exact Q-1026 failure), a hand-kept candidate list, a dead copy left behind unused, a seventh
predicate copy, the uid folded into the shared rule, a narrowed walk, and two widenings of the money
rule itself.

## 2026-10-14 — Q-1035 + Q-1036: two money facts the system stated wrongly

One class, taken from build report 9c612cdb: **a statement about money that the code never checked.**
One was a test asserting a property of arithmetic; the other a field asserting a fact about the wallet.

### Q-1035 — a test that could not fail

It read:

```ts
const twice = realProviderCostUsd([...ENTRIES, ENTRIES[1]]);
expect(Math.abs(twice - REPORT.realCostUsd)).toBeGreaterThan(1e-6);
```

`realProviderCostUsd` is a SUM over its argument. Handing a sum an extra entry changes the total —
that is a property of addition, not of this system, and it holds however the ledger behaves. The test
was NAMED for a claim about the ledger ("the fast lane's GLM is counted ONCE") while asserting
something arithmetic could not disprove. **A test that cannot fail is worse than no test: it produces
exactly the confidence a real double count would need in order to pass unnoticed.**

**And the simulation was wrong in principle too**, which is why it could never have caught the bug
even by accident: the ledger keys its slices by provider + model + phase, so recording the same GLM
turn twice yields **one slice with doubled tokens** — never the two separate entries the array
modelled. The shape it watched for cannot occur.

The claim is now checked where it lives. The report's cost is reproduced through
`createProviderUsageLedger` itself, and a ledger fed one extra GLM turn is asserted to merge into one
slice with doubled tokens, to **say so** in `callsByProvider()`, and to cost more — so a double count
cannot hide behind a plausible total.

⚠️ **Deliberately not asserted: how many GLM calls the real build logged.** Q-1003 records GLM
crawling TWICE on this very report, so "GLM answered once" is not a verified fact, and the test no
longer implies it. `ENTRIES` are the report's merged slices; the call count is a property of the
test's own construction, used only to prove a double record is detectable.

### Q-1036 — `charged` claimed the wallet moved, and never looked

The doc said *"this build's bill was set against the user's wallet"* — a claim about the WALLET —
while the value is `billing applies && bill > 0`, a claim about the BILL. The gap is real money:

- At the settle the debit runs under `if (userId && effectiveBilledUsd > 0 && billingActive)`. When
  `debitRes.ok` is false the failure goes to **`console.error` only** and `walletDebit` stays null —
  and the record still said `charged`, about a bill the balance never paid.
- The watchdog path skips its debit whenever it cannot reproduce the settle's exact `buildRef`,
  deliberately, because a mismatch there could double-charge. Recorded identically.

🔑 **`charged`'s computation is unchanged, on purpose.** Making it require a known debit would have
made every caller that cannot see one report "not charged" about a build that really was billed — one
lie traded for another, which the 2026-09-13 rule forbids outright. The wallet fact is reported
beside it: `walletDebited`, `billedButNotDebited`, and `· billed but NOT debited` on the label, on
every branch that can be charged.

**An unknown stays silent.** "We did not check" and "it did not happen" are different facts and only
the second is a finding, so the settle (which knows the debit result) passes it and the watchdog
(which builds its label before its own debit) passes nothing. A test asserts the field is *absent*
there, not false.

### Proof, and one honest correction to my own method

`tests/aBillTheWalletNeverTookIsSaid.test.ts` (11 tests), plus the existing branch table now pinning
the new flag on EVERY branch — a flag only one test looks at is a flag that quietly becomes true
somewhere nobody checked.

Four reversions: an unknown reported as a missed debit (5 tests fail); the note computed but never
written on the record (2); a bill of zero counted as money owed (1); the settle no longer passing the
fact (1).

🔴 **The second of those first PASSED, and the cause was my own reversion, not a blind test.** The
`replace` carried no assertion, so when it failed to match it silently changed nothing and the green
meant only that I had edited no code. Re-applied with an assertion, it fails two tests. **A reversion
that passes is a claim to verify, never a result to accept** — and that applies to the reversion as
much as to the test.

## 2026-10-14 — Q-1024 + Q-1032 + Q-1034: the platform says only what it checked

Three rows from report 9c612cdb, one class: **a sentence shown to a user that states something the
code never established.**

### Q-1024 — "your app is built", on a build that built nothing

The defect is narrower and worse than the row describes: **the rule already existed, and was enforced
at one of two call sites.** The comment beside `etaFinalChecks = true` states it outright —

> *"The line is announced at once only over an app that exists: a stopped or empty build is never told
> 'your app is built'."*

— and the immediate announcement really does enforce it, via
`emitEtaPhaseNow({ unlessStopped: abort.signal, wrote: builderWroteCount })`, with its own test pinning
that guard. **The two-minute heartbeat tick had no guard at all**, so it said the sentence anyway.
A rule enforced at one of two call sites is not enforced.

So the fact moved into the **sentence**: `finalChecksEtaLine(elapsedMs, appExists)`, defaulting to
claiming nothing. A future caller cannot leak the claim by forgetting a guard, because there is no
guard to forget.

🔑 **The evidence bar was already sitting next to it.** `appRunningEtaLine` demands a real
`appRenderedAt` to say the weaker *"running in the preview"*. The stronger *"your app is built"* must
not be reachable on **less** — and a phase flag is less. Either real fact now earns it (the builder's
own files, or a proven render); neither leaves the line asserting it.

### Q-1032 — a reason that names a file the project does not have

`testSkeletonsCanRun` answers `false` for a package.json that declares no vitest **and** for no
package.json at all (`JSON.parse(String(null))` throws into its `catch`). Both were reported as
*"vitest is not declared in package.json"*. **A false reason is worse than a vague one: it is
actionable in the wrong direction**, sending a reader to add a dependency to a file that is not there.

Three distinct reasons now, deliberately not merged into one vague line, because the fixes differ: one
project needs a dependency, another needs a package.json before that question can be asked, and a
third has a package.json that cannot be parsed.

🔴 **An existing test pinned the defect.** It asserted
`starterTestsSkipReason({ packageJson: null, … }) === STARTER_TESTS_NEED_VITEST`. That expectation was
changed — with the reasoning written beside it in the test — because this row *is* the decision that
the pinned behaviour is wrong. Changing a test to match broken behaviour is forbidden; changing one
that encodes a defect, once the defect is named, is the fix. The difference is whether it is argued or
done quietly.

### Q-1034 — and rule 3 found three siblings the row never named

The row named one internal id ("build 9c612cdb") in `AppKnowledgeBase`, the file **every** AI reads to
answer users. A sweep found `build 46e2d74b` three more times — twice in description text an AI can
repeat aloud. Those are gone. The third is a **code comment**, and it stays on purpose: CLAUDE.md keeps
comments as the audit trail and deliberately does not sweep them.

The tests sentence also now tells a user where *their own* reason is (`⋮ More → Report`) instead of
gesturing at "the build report".

### Proof

`tests/thePlatformSaysOnlyWhatItChecked.test.ts`, 12 tests. The Q-1034 census strips comments and then
asserts **no** internal id survives — with a vacuity guard asserting the comments' own ids are still
present, so the sweep is proven *scoped* rather than blind.

Four reversions, each failing the right test: the sentence defaulting to the claim again; the heartbeat
losing its fact; the three starter-test reasons collapsing back into one; and an internal id returning
to the knowledge text.
## 2026-10-14 — Q-1011: a model call made outside the loop was not on the record (and its deadline could not cancel it)

Two defects in one function, `AgentRunner`'s `endgameBatchRepair`.

**It was invisible.** It calls `client.runTurn` directly, outside the step loop where the three
`onLlmCall` emitters live, so the endgame's batched repair — a call that can spend a minute and a
large prompt — left **no row at all**, on success or on failure. Every autopsy reads `llmCalls`, so
the one place a reader would look to ask "what did the endgame actually do?" was empty.

It now goes through one `recordOffLoopCall`, used on **both** outcomes, because a failed call is a
call that was paid for. The recorder deliberately **invents nothing**: no `answerMs`, `fallbackMs`,
`openMs` or `stopCause`, since those are the loop's own measurements, and putting unmeasured numbers
into a report is this row's defect one level down.

**Its deadline could not cancel it, and that is the expensive half.** `withDeadline` hands a signal to
`runEndgameRepair`, which checks it *between* steps — but the repair passed `this.opts.signal` (the
BUILD's) down to the model. So once the 150 s deadline fired, the call carried on burning tokens for
an answer nothing would read. **A deadline that cannot cancel is a comment.**

🔑 **The fix does not trade Stop for the deadline.** Handing the deadline's signal down *alone* would
have stopped a user's Stop from reaching the call — problem A fixed by creating problem X.
`withDeadline` already accepts a `parent`, so the build's signal is passed as that parent and the one
signal fires on **either**. Both call sites are asserted, not just the function.

**A sibling, found by rule 3.** `tscErrorCause`'s guard pinned `io.llmRepair(out2 + causes, subset)`
*including the closing paren*, so adding a third argument failed a guard whose property was perfectly
intact — the same class as `aModuleIsNotTheWholeApp`'s review-gate guard (fixed yesterday). Repaired
the same way, and proven still to catch its own bug: dropping the annotation fails three tests.

**Proof.** `tests/aCallOutsideTheLoopIsStillOnTheRecord.test.ts`, 7 tests, including a census over
`client.runTurn(` **bodies** so a third site that records nothing fails it. Five reversions, each
failing the right test: the success row removed, the failure row removed, the model call ignoring the
deadline, the deadline losing its parent, and the contract dropping the signal. Two of my own
assertions were wrong on the first run (my recorder is itself a fourth `onLlmCall` site; `codeOnly`
strips the very inline comment I was asserting) — fixed in the test, not in the code.

**Still open, stated rather than implied:** the ROUTE's own direct `runTurn` aux calls (plan,
blueprint, judge) are also absent from `llmCalls`. Their *tokens* are reconciled as `other` by design,
so money is safe; the *rows* are not. A separate change.

## 2026-10-14 — Q-1012 is BLOCKED, because the row's prescribed fix collides with a standing lesson

The row asks for a provider stall ended by our per-turn timeout to be counted in
`PROVIDER_TIME_WASTED`. Investigating it found the opposite rule already written down, in
`providerWaste.ts`'s own header, from autopsy bb688add:

> *"OUR OWN CLOCK ENDING IS NOT A PROVIDER'S WASTE … a lane that ran out of ITS budget mid-call is our
> accounting, not the vendor's failure."*

The per-turn timeout **is** our clock. Counting it as vendor waste would re-introduce exactly what
that autopsy removed — and this number is what the 429 bench's trigger will be re-chosen from, so
inflating it would move a routing decision on a false reading.

The honest distinction is whether the provider was *producing* when our clock fired: `crawl` and
`silent` are real vendor waste, a healthy call our budget cut short is not. **That fact is not
available at the timeout site** — there is no `TurnResult`, so no `firstOutputAfterMs` or
`openedAfterMs`, and the chain does not report which rung was serving when a stop cancels it.

So it is recorded as BLOCKED with all four fields, with the recommendation to count it only as
`silent` (provider produced nothing) and never as `timeout`, and with the note that the required
change is inside the provider chain — which CLAUDE.md says to confirm with the admin before touching.
Guessing it would put a number nobody measured into the figure a routing decision is made from.

## 2026-10-14 — Q-1042: the evidence half, built; and Q-1043, the defect it uncovered

### Q-1042 — the hunt's cost, on every build instead of one archaeological read

The admin's instinct about the post-build review is right — *"aap help ko glm se chalo to sayad sasta
chale?"* — and the figure behind it is real: *"523,374 input tokens = 34.4% of the build … billed at
×4"*. But that figure came from reading **one** report **by hand**. A routing decision taken from one
anecdote is a guess with a citation.

🔴 **Routing was deliberately not touched.** `cheapBuildFloorRunners` carries **six** separate verbatim
admin routing decisions, with env overrides that always win, and CLAUDE.md says to confirm before
changing any of it. The admin asked *"sayad sasta chale?"* — a question, not a decision. So the row is
BLOCKED on their yes, and what shipped is the half that makes the yes informed: `bugHuntCost.ts` puts
the hunt's share of each build's engine cost into every report.

**Three things the line deliberately does not do**, each for a reason this repo has already paid for:

- **It names no engine.** The build report reaches the USER (⋮ More → Report), and the White-Label Law
  is absolute. The share answers the question anyway — 34.4% is what made the point.
- **It states no per-slice ₹.** The markup (then the discount) applies to the build's **total**, not to
  each slice, so a rupee figure for the hunt would be a number nobody computed — Q-1035's class exactly.
- **It says nothing when the hunt did not run.** A "0%" line would read as a hunt that found nothing for
  free; Q-1040's not-run principle one level on.

Priced by `realProviderCostUsd` — the one cost function — with the share's numerator **and** denominator
from the same call, so the ratio can never compare two differently-priced numbers.

### Q-1043 — found by rule 3 while adding the sibling, and it was mine

`BUG_HUNT_NOT_RUN`, which **I shipped in #3728**, was in no registry at all. `isAppFinding` reads only
the phase and `PROCESS_ONLY_CODES` — `severity: 'info'` and `autoResolved: true` do not help — so it
said **yes**. And `BuildDiagnostics.ts` already records what that costs, from the 2026-10-04 census:

> *"Eight codes recorded at WARNING severity that were in no registry at all, so `isAppFinding` said yes
> to every one: each appeared in the USER's build-health card as a problem with THEIR app and took 6
> points off their app's health score."*

**So a person who pressed "Not now" on a paid extra was losing app-health points for declining to pay.**
Both codes are now process-only and carry no "next move", because a choice is not a defect and a cost is
not a next move.

🔒 **The class is locked, not the instance.** The test scans the route and `optionalBugHunt.ts` for every
`code: 'BUG_HUNT_*'` actually recorded and asserts each one is process-only — so a third code added the
way #3728 added the first fails CI instead of quietly costing a user six points.

### Proof, and the reversion that taught me something

`tests/whatTheHuntCostIsSaidAndIsNotTheAppsFault.test.ts`, 14 tests. Six reversions: the #3728 defect put
back; a vendor name in the user-visible line; a per-slice rupee figure; no zero-cost guard; a cost line
for a hunt that never ran; and a third `BUG_HUNT_*` code left unregistered.

🔴 **One reversion PASSED, and chasing it found a real hole in my own guard.** The source guard listed
the honest FUNCTIONS (`usdInrRate`, `tieredMarkupUsd`), so a hardcoded `realUsd * 88 * 4` walked straight
past it — **it knew every honest way to get a rupee and not one dishonest way.** Widened to the rupee
sign. The first attempt, `[₹$]`, failed the *correct* code because every template literal contains
`${…}`; scoped to `₹` and re-proven. Two lessons, both already paid for today: a reversion that passes is
a claim to verify, and a guard written from the honest implementations is blind to the dishonest ones.

## 2026-10-14 — Wallet & Billing redesign: three pages, one balance (branch `claude/wallet-billing-redesign`)

**What the admin asked for** (an external brief + three mock-ups, handled under the external-suggestion rule: adapted to the
real code, not transcribed). Wallet & Billing becomes exactly three pages — **Buy Tokens · Promo Code · History** — mobile
first, simple English, every number from the real backend.

**What shipped.** `BillingPanel.tsx` is now a header (`WalletHeader`: balance + the three tabs) over one page at a time:
`TokenPurchaseTab` (quick amounts + the amount box + one Pay button + recent payments with an honest status),
`PromoRewardsTab` (referral code/steps via the existing `ReferralPanel`, the friends list, the promo box, gift codes behind
one tap) and `WalletStatementPanel` (the reconciled history with filters, a time range and "Show more"). Hosting plans,
add-ons, today's usage and the month's AI cost moved under ONE collapsed "Plans, add-ons and usage" section. Pure logic is in
`walletTabs.ts`, `walletQuickAmounts.ts`, `walletHistoryView.ts`, `walletPaymentRows.ts`, `referredFriendsView.ts`.
**Nothing about money changed**: the order is still created by `onCreateBillingOrder`, store packs by `onBuyStorePack`, the
coupon by `onRedeemPromoCoupon`, tokens are credited only by the server after the gateway confirms; App.tsx is untouched
(the page is chosen through the `activeBillingDetailTab` it already owns — `walletTabs.ts` maps its four values to three pages).

**Where the brief was CORRECTED against the code (rule 3 — honesty, not obedience):**
| Brief / mock-up said | The code does | What was built |
|---|---|---|
| ₹100 = 10,000 tokens | the 2% platform fee comes off first: ₹100 → **9,800** tokens | chips print tokens from the server's own `splitPaymentAtPct`; a test pins 9,800 ≠ 10,000 |
| a Cashfree / Google Play radio | the rail is decided by the platform (web gateway; Play packs REPLACE it by Play policy; iPhone cannot buy) | no radio; "UPI, cards or net banking" with no vendor name (White-Label Law); the iPhone notice still never points outside |
| referrer earns 100 tokens after 4/4 steps | the referrer earns ₹25 per friend verification (email, mobile, GitHub; ₹75/friend, ₹1,500 total); the user's own 5 steps pay ₹100 each | the real rules, from the server; no ₹ is derived per friend (the server gates, caps and pays exactly-once) |
| Devanagari / Hinglish labels | CLAUDE.md language standard + `uiLanguageEnglishOnly` | simple English |
| friend names and emails in the list | a referrer may see PROGRESS, not collect addresses | the server now sends a **masked label** only (`fr••••••@mail.com`; 1–2 letter names reveal nothing); the raw `email` field is gone from `/referred` and from the profile "Earning" sheet |

**Root causes found on the way (class → fix → lock):**
- *A balance that could not be read printed as 0* (`wallet?.tokenBalance ?? 0`). → `readableBalance` + "Could not load / Try again". Lock: `theWalletHeaderNeverShowsAFalseZero` (+ a source ban on `tokenBalance ?? 0` in every wallet file).
- *A pending or failed payment looked like a purchase.* → `walletPaymentRows`: only an explicit `SUCCESS` is "paid", anything unreadable is "waiting". Lock: `walletPaymentRows.test.ts`.
- *A filter can hide money.* → every history row belongs to exactly one filter; counts add up to All; an unreadable date is KEPT by every range. Lock: `walletHistoryView.test.ts`.
- *The `maskEmail` self-view mask prints a whole 1–2 letter address* if reused for a third party. → `referralFriendLabel` (a third, at most two characters). Lock: `aReferredFriendIsNeverNamedByAddress`.
- *A source-pinned test cannot see a layout.* The structural measurement passed while two real defects were visible only in screenshots (a selected chip and a verdict banner rendering as solid fills). Both turned out to be the HARNESS serving Vite's dev CSS (the repo's postcss `cascade-layers` fallback rule beats the later `@supports color-mix` rule only in dev); re-measured against the production CSS: clean. Recorded so nobody re-chases it.
- Three source-pin tests were re-pointed to the new files with their intent kept (`appLockWiring`, `platformFee`, `theIphoneCannotOpenACheckout`, `theApplyButtonStaysOnScreen`, `everyValueTheAppKeepsIsRead`, `theRedDotLeadsToTheTopUp`); the capsule-row cases were superseded by `theWalletTabsFitAPhone` (tab bar, 44px targets, tokens-only colour, wrapping).

**Measured, not assumed:** a real Chromium against the PRODUCTION css, 5 widths (320/360/375/390/430) × 7 states (buy, Play packs, iPhone, unread balance, promo, history, history error): no horizontal scroll, no clipped text, every control ≥ 44px — 35/35 clean; light, dark and 320px screenshots read by eye.
**Reversion-proven (5):** label leaks the address · unknown status shown as paid · unread balance shown as 0 · a filter drops a kind · the route sends the raw email — each made its test fail; restored.

**Left open, honestly (none is a silent gap):**
1. 🟡 *Decision for the admin:* the profile "Earning" sheet used to show friends' FULL emails because the admin asked for it (2026-09). It is now masked, per this brief's privacy rule. Say if the full address is wanted back.
2. The date range and "Show more" are client-side over the ≤500 rows the statement already returns — there is no server pagination to call.
3. History shows tokens only; the old "₹" running balance columns became "Balance after: N" (tokens).
4. `/transactions` returns the latest 50 payments, so "Your recent payments" is bounded to those (it shows the latest 5).
5. A "Payment did not go through" row does not say "you were not charged" — the record cannot prove that, so it does not claim it.

## 2026-10-14 — iOS release build #111 failed at the Google Sign-In wiring; fixed at the class (branch `fix/ios-scene-delegate-google-signin`)

**Report.** The `.ipa` build the admin asked for (`ios-ipa.yml`, run #111, `main` @ 8b4d727) stopped in 1.5 minutes at the step "Wire the
Google Sign-In redirect into AppDelegate" with its own message — *"AppDelegate patch failed — the template changed"*. The same-day Android run (#152)
built, signed and uploaded to the Play internal track (every step green, including "Upload to Google Play (internal track)").

**Root cause.** The step patched `AppDelegate.application(_:open:options:)`. Capacitor 8.5.x (bumped in #3666, after the last good iOS build on 2026-10-08)
generates a UIScene-lifecycle project: `AppDelegate` has no `open url` method any more and the redirect arrives in `SceneDelegate.scene(_:openURLContexts:)`.
Verified by running `npx cap add ios` and reading the output. The guard did its job (it stopped, it did not ship an app whose Google login hangs forever).

**Class.** *A patch applied to a generated template whose anchor is checked only when it ships.* Every edit `ios-ipa.yml` makes to what Capacitor generates is
anchored to the template's shape, and a dependency bump moves the shape with no line of ours changing.

**Fix, and why it is a class fix.**
- `scripts/ios-wire-google-signin.sh` (new): knows BOTH templates (classic → AppDelegate, UIScene → SceneDelegate, the URL offered to `GIDSignIn` before the
  Capacitor proxy and consumed when handled), is idempotent, uses portable perl (no BSD `sed -i ''`), and exits 1 with an `::error::` on a THIRD shape — never a silent skip.
  The workflow step now calls it; there is no second inline copy to drift.
- `tests/theIosTemplateStillHasEveryAnchorTheWorkflowPatches.test.ts` runs the REAL `npx cap add ios` in CI (no network, no macOS needed — verified) and holds every
  anchor the workflow depends on (files, the AppIcon set, the Xcode project, the AppDelegate closing brace the APNs step inserts before, and exactly-one-of-two redirect
  anchors), runs the script for real on the generated template AND on a classic fixture, and proves the "neither template" refusal. The next Capacitor bump that moves an
  anchor fails the PR that bumps it, not a release on a macOS runner. Reverted-and-failed: breaking the Scene branch fails the test; restored.
- Siblings hunted: the push-notification step also edits `AppDelegate.swift` — its anchor (insert before the class's final brace) still holds on the new template and is now tested.

**Honest limit (rule 6).** No Xcode here, so the Swift cannot be compiled in this session; the injected code is guarded by `#if canImport(GoogleSignIn)` and
read against the generated template. The real proof is the iOS run itself, and — because the failure this wiring prevents ("Google login succeeds → redirect back →
infinite loading") only shows on a device — **the TestFlight build needs one real Google sign-in on an iPhone before it is promoted.**

**Addendum (same day, #3740's own first CI run).** The new template test first ran `npx cap add ios` and PASSED locally but FAILED in CI: `ci.yml` is on **Node 20** and
`@capacitor/cli` 8 requires **Node >= 22** (`[fatal] The Capacitor CLI requires NodeJS >=22.0.0`, reproduced with `/opt/node20`). The test now unpacks the two iOS template
tarballs Capacitor ships (`ios-spm-template` — what `cap add ios` generates — and `ios-pods-template`, which still carries the classic AppDelegate redirect), so it needs no CLI, no
Node 22 and no network; the generated `AppDelegate.swift`/`SceneDelegate.swift` were compared byte for byte with the SPM tarball's first. Verified under Node 20 and by reversion (breaking the
Scene branch fails it; restored). **New open row Q-1060:** CI tests Node 20 while production and every release workflow run Node 22 — a gate exercising a runtime nobody ships. Not fixed here: moving 38,000 tests
to Node 22 is its own change (run the suite on 22 first, then flip `ci.yml`).
